# FIT5145 Assignment 1 & 3: Data-Driven Pacing Corridor for HYROX Athletes

## Dataset Source

In this demonstration, the datasets are obtained by websrcaping and saved into csv files named:

- hyrox_season8_male_pro.csv
- hyrox_season8_female_pro.csv

These datasets has been published to excelyynxl-a11 GitHub repository (link: <https://github.com/excelyynxl-a11y/fit5145/tree/main/ass1_3>). You can download the csv files and saved them into a data folder to carry out this demonstration.

## Load library

```{R}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(hms)
library(caret)
library(grid)
```

## Load dataset

Season 8 Male Pro dataset.

```{R}
szn8_male_pro <- read_csv("data/hyrox_season8_male_pro.csv")
glimpse(szn8_male_pro)
```

Season 8 Female Pro dataset.

```{R}
szn8_female_pro <- read_csv("data/hyrox_season8_female_pro.csv")
glimpse(szn8_female_pro)
```

## Data cleaning

### Inspect szn8_male_pro

Convert all time split into \<time\> format

```{R}
# Define all split columns
run_cols <- paste0("Running_", 1:8)
station_cols <- c(
  "SkiErg_1000m", 
  "Sled_Push_50m", 
  "Sled_Pull_50m",
  "Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m", 
  "Row_1000m", 
  "Farmers_Carry_200m",
  "Sandbag_Lunges_100m", 
  "Wall_Balls"
)
all_time_cols <- c("Total_Time", "Roxzone_Time", run_cols, station_cols)

```

```{R}
# Standardize all time columns to strict <time> (hms class)
time_fomatted_male <- szn8_male_pro %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(all_time_cols),
      ~ if (inherits(.x, "hms") || inherits(.x, "difftime")) {
        hms::as_hms(as.numeric(.x))
      } else {
        hms::as_hms(period_to_seconds(lubridate::hms(as.character(.x))))
      }
    )
  )

# Verify that all time split are of <time>
glimpse(time_fomatted_male[all_time_cols])
```

Check for any NA values

```{R}
time_fomatted_male %>% filter(if_any(everything(), is.na))
```

We observed 784 rows contain NA values. Since only a small fraction (784 out of 12400 rows) of cases have several missings, we will drop these cases.

Check distinct City.

```{R}
time_fomatted_male %>% group_by(City) %>% summarise(count = n())
```

We observe the oddness that all City are recorded as "N/A" as characters instead of true NA values. Since City is totally missing for all entries and does not carry significance to the analysis, we will drop the City variable.

Check distinct Division.

```{R}
time_fomatted_male %>% group_by(Division) %>% summarise(count = n())
```

We observe that all athletes are HYROX PRO Division (ignore NA since it will be dropped later), which is correct based on our project scope. For easy gender reference, we will add a "MALE" remark – "MALE HYROX PRO".

Based on all inspection made, we will now clean szn8_male_pro and saved into a new male_pro_clean.

```{R}
male_pro_clean <- time_fomatted_male %>%
  # drop all NA cases
  filter(!if_any(everything(), is.na)) %>%
  # deselect City and athlete_url column
  select(- City, - athlete_url) %>%
  # remark MALE in Division
  mutate(
    Division = "MALE HYROX PRO"
  )
  

male_pro_clean %>% head()
```

### Inspect szn8_female_pro

Data cleaning approach is similar as szn8_female_pro.

```{R}
# Standardize all time columns to strict <time> (hms class)
time_fomatted_female <- szn8_female_pro %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(all_time_cols),
      ~ if (inherits(.x, "hms") || inherits(.x, "difftime")) {
        hms::as_hms(as.numeric(.x))
      } else {
        hms::as_hms(period_to_seconds(lubridate::hms(as.character(.x))))
      }
    )
  )

# Verify that all time split are of <time>
glimpse(time_fomatted_female)
```

```{R}
time_fomatted_female %>% filter(if_any(everything(), is.na))
```

Dropping cases and imputing values.

```{R}
female_pro_clean <- time_fomatted_female %>%
  # drop all NA cases
  filter(!if_any(everything(), is.na)) %>%
  # deselect City and athlete_url column
  select(- City, - athlete_url) %>%
  # remark FEMALE in Division
  mutate(
    Division = "FEMALE HYROX PRO"
  )


female_pro_clean %>% head()
```

### Combining male and female into a single dataset

```{R}
combined_pro_clean <- bind_rows(
  male_pro_clean,
  female_pro_clean
)

glimpse(combined_pro_clean)
```

Check if both male and female data exist in combined dataset.

```{R}
combined_pro_clean %>% filter(Division == "MALE HYROX PRO") %>% head()
```

```{R}
combined_pro_clean %>% filter(Division == "FEMALE HYROX PRO") %>% head()
```

Both MALE and FEMALE data exist in the combined dataset.

## Exploratory Data Analysis

For EDA as part of descriptive analysis, we will reveal the run time in relation to their station, relationship between early run mean and later run mean.

### 1. Running trajectory and slowdown

```{R}
combined_long <- combined_pro_clean %>%
  select(
    Division,
    starts_with("Running_")
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Running_"),
    names_to = "Run_Name",
    values_to = "Run_Time"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Run_Num = as.numeric(str_extract(Run_Name, "\\d+")),
    Time_Sec = as.numeric(Run_Time) # Time split of each run in seconds
  )

combined_long %>% head()
```

Generate summary of running Q1, Q2 or median, Q3

```{R}
run_summary <- combined_long %>%
  group_by(Division, Run_Num) %>%
  summarise(
    Q1_Sec    = quantile(Time_Sec, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median_Sec = median(Time_Sec, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q3_Sec    = quantile(Time_Sec, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    Coef_Variation = sd(Time_Sec) / mean(Time_Sec), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )
  
run_summary %>% arrange(Run_Num)
```

Visualize median run split time with interquartile range against run station with a line chart.

```{R}
ggplot(run_summary, aes(x = Run_Num, y = Median_Sec, color = Division, fill = Division, group = Division)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q1_Sec, ymax = Q3_Sec), alpha = 0.25, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  # Vertical dashed line after Run 4
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.7) +
  # Differentiate colour based on division
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FEMALE HYROX PRO" ="#E377C2", "MALE HYROX PRO" = "#1F77B4")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FEMALE HYROX PRO" = "#E377C2", "MALE HYROX PRO" = "#1F77B4")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8, labels = paste("Run", 1:8)) +
  labs(
    title = "HYROX Run-Time Trajectory",
    subtitle = "Median run split times with interquartile range; Dashed line marks mid-race",
    x = "Run Segment",
    y = "Split Time (seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray30")
  )
```

A general observation we see is female split time is higher than males. The overall trend of split time as the race progresses is almost identical across both division – run split time increases per station.

### 2. Slowdown summary and early–later association

Here, we want to analyse if early run split time is associated to later run split time.

```{R}
analysis_data <- combined_pro_clean %>%
  mutate(
    # Time split of all run station to seconds
    Running_1 = as.numeric(Running_1),
    Running_2 = as.numeric(Running_2),
    Running_3 = as.numeric(Running_3),
    Running_4 = as.numeric(Running_4),
    Running_5 = as.numeric(Running_5),
    Running_6 = as.numeric(Running_6),
    Running_7 = as.numeric(Running_7),
    Running_8 = as.numeric(Running_8),
    # Time split of all functional station to seconds
    SkiErg_1000m = as.numeric(SkiErg_1000m),
    Sled_Push_50m = as.numeric(Sled_Push_50m),
    Sled_Pull_50m = as.numeric(Sled_Pull_50m),
    Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m = as.numeric(Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m),
    Row_1000m = as.numeric(Row_1000m),
    Farmers_Carry_200m = as.numeric(Farmers_Carry_200m),
    Sandbag_Lunges_100m = as.numeric(Sandbag_Lunges_100m),
    Wall_Balls = as.numeric(Wall_Balls),
    # Total time to seconds
    Total_Time = as.numeric(Total_Time),
    Early_Run_Mean = rowMeans(across(all_of(run_cols[1:4]), as.numeric), na.rm = TRUE),
    Later_Run_Mean = rowMeans(across(all_of(run_cols[5:8]), as.numeric), na.rm = TRUE),
    Slowdown_Percentage = 100 * (Later_Run_Mean - Early_Run_Mean) / Early_Run_Mean
  )

analysis_data %>% select(Name, Early_Run_Mean, Later_Run_Mean) %>% head()
```

The slowdown percentage quantifies pace collapse. The median athlete slows by about 7.6% from the early to the later half in both divisions, with a long right tail of severe collapses.

```{R}
slowdown_summary <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(Division) %>%
  summarise(
    Median_Slowdown_Pct = median(Slowdown_Percentage),
    Q1_Slowdown_Pct = quantile(Slowdown_Percentage, 0.25),
    Q3_Slowdown_Pct = quantile(Slowdown_Percentage, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

slowdown_summary
```

Histogram is used to show the distribution of slowdown percentage from early run mean (Runs 1-4) to later run mean (Runs 5-8). A slowdown percentage exceeding right of dashed line (0%) means athletes slowed down in second half run.

```{R}
ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = Slowdown_Percentage, fill = Division)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FEMALE HYROX PRO" = "#E377C2", "MALE HYROX PRO" = "#1F77B4")) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Pace Collapse",
    subtitle = "Slowdown percentage from early run mean (Runs 1-4) to later run mean (Runs 5-8)",
    x = "Slowdown (%)",
    y = "Athletes",
    fill = "Division"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Division, nrow = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray30")
  )
```

## Correlation Analysis

Spearman rank correlation is used to assess the strength and direction of association between continuous variables as split times are non-normal, continuous and less affected by extreme outliers.

Spearman rank correlation between later run mean with each possible half-race factors: early run mean and first 4 functional stations (SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump) to determine the strength of correlation.

```{R}
early_spearman_summary <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(Division) %>%
  summarise(
    Run_Spearman = cor(Early_Run_Mean, Later_Run_Mean, method = "spearman"),
    Ski_Spearman = cor(SkiErg_1000m, Later_Run_Mean, method = "spearman"),
    SPush_Spearman = cor(Sled_Push_50m, Later_Run_Mean, method = "spearman"),
    SPull_Spearman = cor(Sled_Pull_50m, Later_Run_Mean, method = "spearman"),
    BBJ_Spearman = cor(Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m, Later_Run_Mean, method = "spearman"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_Spearman"),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Rvalue"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Predictor = str_remove(Predictor, "_Spearman")
  ) %>%
  arrange(Division, desc(Rvalue))

early_spearman_summary
```

For females, early run mean correlates strongest with later run mean (r=0.742), followed by burpee broad jump (r=0.266) and sled pull (r=0.200). For males, the same ordering holds (r=0.652, 0.150 and 0.100 respectively). The remaining stations show near-zero correlations, ranking last and entering the model ladder only in Model 4. The ranking orders the candidate linear regression model The remaining stations show weak-to-near-zero correlations (SkiErg: 0.128 female, -0.005 male; Sled Push: 0.091 female, 0.015 male), ranking last and therefore entering the model ladder only in Model 4.

Below is a stacked scatterplot of later run mean versus early run mean with a linear trend line.

```{R}
ggplot(analysis_data, 
       aes(
         x = Early_Run_Mean, 
         y = Later_Run_Mean, 
         color = Division)
      ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", e = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ Division, nrow = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FEMALE HYROX PRO" = "#E377C2", "MALE HYROX PRO" = "#1F77B4")) +
  labs(
    title = "Later Run Mean versus Early Run Mean",
    x = "Mean Runs 1–4 (seconds)",
    y = "Mean Runs 5–8 (seconds)",
    color = "Division"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray30")
  )
```

From above, we see a clear linear trend across both division. This hints us that the predictive analysis can use a linear regression to produce a model that predicts later run mean from early run mean.

## Linear Regression

The goal is to produce a model that with closest prediction on later-run performance (mean of Runs 5–8) at the mid-race checkpoint using a single or a combination of factors from: early run mean (run 1-4) and first 4 functional stations (SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump).

First, we will produce 4 linear regression models:

- Model 1: early run mean only

- Model 2: combination of early run mean with burpee broad jump

- Model 3: combination of early run mean with burpee broad jump and sled pull

- Model 4: combination of early mean run and all 4 functional stations.

Afterwards, we will analyse the 4 linear regression model diagnostics by their residual vs fitted to check for non-linearity and homoscedasticity (constant variance of residuals). This step is to check if we potentially need to transform variables (into log, square root or polynomial).

Then, we compare and evaluate the 4 models using cross-validation based on RMSE, R2 and MAE.

Lastly, we conclude the best models and suggest alternative division-based model is required.

### A) Model 1: early run mean only

```{R}
model1 <- lm(Later_Run_Mean ~ Early_Run_Mean * Division, data = analysis_data)

summary(model1)
```

### B) Model 2: early run mean + burpee broad jump

```{R}
model2 <- lm(Later_Run_Mean ~ (Early_Run_Mean + Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m) * Division, data = analysis_data)

summary(model2)
```

### C) Model 3: early run mean + burpee broad jump +sled pull

```{R}
model3 <- lm(Later_Run_Mean ~ (Early_Run_Mean + Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m + Sled_Pull_50m) * Division, data = analysis_data)

summary(model3)
```

### D) Model 4: early run mean + all 4 functional stations

```{R}
model4 <- lm(Later_Run_Mean ~ (Early_Run_Mean + Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m + Sled_Pull_50m + SkiErg_1000m + Sled_Push_50m) * Division, data = analysis_data)

summary(model4)
```

## Linear regression diagnostics using residual vs fitted plot

```{R}
# Helper function to create individual ggplots
make_diag_plot <- function(model, title_name) {
  # Fitted = x-value, Residual = y-value
  df <- tibble(
    Fitted = fitted(model),
    Residual = resid(model)
  )
  
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Fitted, y = Residual)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.9) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    labs(title = title_name, x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals") +
    theme_minimal()
}

# Generate individual plots
p1 <- make_diag_plot(model1, "Model 1")
p2 <- make_diag_plot(model2, "Model 2")
p3 <- make_diag_plot(model3, "Model 3")
p4 <- make_diag_plot(model4, "Model 4")

# Draw and display the 2x2 layout on screen (run all in on go)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(
  nrow = 3, 
  ncol = 2, 
  heights = unit(c(0.1, 0.45, 0.45), "npc")
)))

grid.text(
  "Residuals vs Fitted Values Across Models", 
  vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1:2),
  gp = gpar(fontsize = 12)
)

print(p1, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(p2, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(p3, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(p4, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 2))
```

All 4 models shows random scatter around horizontal axis with no distinct trends, curved or U-shape. This suggests that all models are well-fitted and capture the linear relationship adequately.

### 

## Model evalutation using cross-validation (10 folds)

```{R}
# Define each models linear formula
f1 <- Later_Run_Mean ~ Early_Run_Mean * Division
f2 <- Later_Run_Mean ~ (Early_Run_Mean + Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m) * Division
f3 <- Later_Run_Mean ~ (Early_Run_Mean + Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m + Sled_Pull_50m) * Division
f4 <- Later_Run_Mean ~ (Early_Run_Mean + Burpee_Broad_Jump_80m + Sled_Pull_50m + SkiErg_1000m + Sled_Push_50m) * Division
```

```{R}
# Set up cross-validation
set.seed(5145) # for reproduceability 

# Put 4 formulas into a list
forms <- list(M1 = f1, M2 = f2, M3 = f3, M4 = f4)

folds <- createFolds(analysis_data$Division, k = 10, returnTrain = TRUE)

train_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10,
  index = folds,
  savePredictions = "final"
)

# Apply train() onto each element in list
fits <- lapply(
  forms,
  function(f)
    train(
      f, 
      data = analysis_data, 
      method = "lm", 
      trControl = train_control
    )
)

cv_results <- bind_rows(
  fits$M1$results,
  fits$M2$results,
  fits$M3$results,
  fits$M4$results,
  .id = "Model"
) %>%
  select(
    Model, RMSE, Rsquared, MAE
  )

cv_results
```

Naive persistence baseline is created with predict later run mean equal to early run mean. This baseline is used to used as a comparison / baseline for a model. It provides a target to evaluate is a model improvement is significant, by how much, make error intepretable and set a target for future work. As simple as it is, it is important in answering:

- Does early-run mean carry any predictive information about slowdown? Or

- Would ignoring the question entirely work just as well?

```{R}
persistence_baseline <- analysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    Persistence_Pred = Early_Run_Mean, #  predict later run mean = early run mean
    Abs_Error = abs(Later_Run_Mean - Persistence_Pred), # how wrong is the naive forecast
    Sq_Error = (Later_Run_Mean - Persistence_Pred)^2
  )

persistence_baseline %>%
  group_by(Division) %>%
  summarise(
    Persistence_RMSE = sqrt(mean(Sq_Error)),
    Persistence_MAE = mean(Abs_Error),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      Division = "OVERALL",
      Persistence_RMSE = sqrt(mean(persistence_baseline$Sq_Error)),
      Persistence_MAE = mean(persistence_baseline$Abs_Error)
    )
  )
```

We observed:

- The naive persistence baseline (predicting later run mean equal to early run mean) yields RMSE = 25.09 and MAE = 20.84 overall. Model 1 improves on this baseline by 36% (RMSE) and 40% (MAE), confirming that early run mean carries genuine information about later-run performance rather than merely echoing the athlete's general pace.

- RMSE and MAE decrease only marginally from model 1 (RMSE=15.96; MAE=12.40) to model 4 (RMSE=15.86; MAE=12.33) — an improvement of about 0.1 seconds. Adding functional stations as factors reduces the difference between prediction and actual value, but the improvement is practically negligible.

- R2 increases from model 1 (R2=0.704) to model 4 (R2=0.708), meaning adding functional stations marginally improves the percentage of how much variation in later run mean is explainable by model. The increment is likewise negligible.

- Since adding more factors does not deliver a substantive improvement, the parsimony principle selects model 1 (early run mean only as predictor of later run mean). Model 1 can explain 70% of variation in later run time, with an average of 12.4s absolute differences between model predictions and athletes' actual later run mean values.

Running carries most of the race's predictive signal, while the first-half functional stations measure distinct physical capacities that correlate only weakly with later-run pace (r = 0.10–0.27). The remaining 30% of unexplained variation reflects factors absent from the data, namely individual fatigue resistance, venue and weather conditions, penalty times embedded in splits and age-group heterogeneity within the pro division.

Model 1 (early run mean only as later run mean predictor) is chosen. To visualise its efficacy, predicted later run mean is plotted against actual later run mean with an identity reference line. The closer the points to the line, the more accurate the forecast.

```{R}
fits$M1$pred %>%
  mutate(
    Division = analysis_data$Division[rowIndex]
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pred, y = obs, colour = Division)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Division, nrow=1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1, 
    intercept = 0, 
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Model 1: Early run mean only",
    x = "Predicted later run mean", 
    y = "Actual later run mean"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{R}
# for conclusion reference
analysis_data %>% group_by(Division) %>%
  summarise(
    Median_Later_Run = median(Later_Run_Mean)
  )
```

## Conclusion

The demonstration evidences the project's feasibility: a mid-race checkpoint forecast of later-run performance is achievable from elapsed splits alone, with an average error of 12.4 seconds — around 5% of the median later-run mean (241 seconds male, 278 seconds female) — using only data that race timing systems already publish. The main limitations are the 30% of variance unexplained by early splits, a small number of extreme slowdown outlier and generalization beyond Season 8 pro fields remaining untested.
